title: US-Canada tariffs: Canada braces for prolonged trade war as counter-tariffs on US take effect
description: Canada's retaliatory tariffs on a range of US goods came into effect on Tuesday, with no sign of a trade deal on the horizon. The counter-tariffs will
body: Canada's retaliatory tariffs on a range of US goods came into effect on Tuesday, with no sign of a trade deal on the horizon. The counter-tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, from steel to furniture to cotton T-shirts, and will be as high as 50%. Fresh fish and lobster were also on the list, but Canada later omitted them after pushback from its seafood industry - a sign of the tricky balance it has to strike as it retaliates against its largest trading partner.Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no movement has been made to resume talks after they collapsed in late August.Speaking to reporters last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada is still in search of a deal with the US that is "durable" and in the best interests of both countries."We're ready to sit down and and strike that deal when the Americans are ready," Carney said.US trade representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said on Thursday that the ball is in Canada's court. "We offered them the best deal, they looked at it square in the face and turned around," Greer said in an interview with Fox News, adding that there has been sparse communication with the Canadians since talks collapsed.In a separate interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC, Greer cautioned against retaliation and suggested the US might hit back by banning the import of some Canadian products.President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to halt all US business with Canada-based airplane maker Bombardier unless it moved its manufacturing south. The company is one of the largest in the country, contributing over C$7bn to Canada's annual GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombarier by public accounting firm PwC. Trump took aim at Canada in a series of other Truth Social posts over the weekend, including one that called Canada's exchange rate with the US "unacceptable".Another post showed a map of North America - including Canada and Mexico - and Greenland all overlaid with the US flag. Canada and the US have the world's largest bilateral trading relationship valued at nearly $900bn in 2025.With new US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs are now in effect, businesses on both side are scrambling to deal with what comes next. The US currently has in place a 25% tax on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as taxes on Canadian steel, aluminium and lumber. In late August, President Donald Trump imposed new 50% tariffs on other goods like dairy, alcohol, hockey sticks and perfume. Canada's counter-tariffs, which were described by Carney as "dollar-for-dollar", will be applied to hundreds of items coming in from the US as of midnight on Tuesday.  They are in addition to existing retaliatory taxes Canada had placed on finished American cars and trucks that are non-compliant with a free trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada.Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support, external their country imposing retaliatory tariffs on the US.But economists warn that the latest counter-tariffs will raise prices for consumers, external on everyday goods like clothing, food and furniture.  The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has also urged the Carney government to take a surgical approach to retaliation. "Businesses understand retaliation but don't want to see endless escalation," said the Chamber's CEO and President Candace Laing in a statement to the BBC on Friday, though she added that businesses "are preparing for this trade dispute to last".Pushback from the fisheries industry was enough for Canada to alter its counter-tariffs by removing dozens of seafood items to avoid unintended consequences to its own economy. The lobster industry in both Canada and the US are heavily dependent on the other, with American-caught lobster often sent to north to be processed before it is shipped back to the US and sold. Ahead of the latest tariffs, Canada's economy had shown signs of resliency. Its GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter and it had gained 181,000 jobs from April to July. But around 41,000 jobs were lost in August, a period that coincided with the new US tariffs on Canada and the collapse in trade talks.One sector that saw a modest bump was manufacturing - a gain the Canadian government attributes to consumers and businesses buying more made-in-Canada products.Prime Minister Carney has vowed to diversify Canada's trade away from the US. July figures show the share of US-bound Canadian exports dropped to 66% from an average of 75% before the trade war.

schema.headline: US-Canada tariffs: Canada braces for prolonged trade war as counter-tariffs on US take effect

title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit
description: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers a
body: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move."During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident."So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice. "I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit."I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X."Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

schema.headline: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit

title: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says
description: Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to
body: Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC). In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.  HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing. Skeer said it was a "pivotal moment for policing" and "there are still areas where performance is not good enough"."If managed correctly, I firmly believe that reform presents a significant opportunity to deliver a better service for both the public and those working within policing," she added.The HMIC report said that evolving crime and threats mean officers deal with more complex and resource-intensive cases.But the government's planned reforms, including the creation of a National Police Service to take over counter-terror and fraud investigations could alleviate some of the pressure facing local units, Skeer wrote.Policing minister Sarah Jones said: "Our plans will tackle the long-term challenges in the policing system and bring it into the modern day. "We are investing in more neighbourhood policing, raising standards and making better use of technology to make sure local policing works for local people."Responding to the report, the charity Victim Support said: "Police forces are undoubtedly under immense pressure, but they must get the basics right." Chief executive Katie Kempen added: "It is unacceptable that victims and survivors are paying the price for police failings. Every victim of crime deserves to be treated with respect, to be given access to justice, and to have their needs identified and met."Growing financial pressure is repeatedly pointed to as increasing the strain on police forces.Cleveland's police's Chief Constable, Victoria Fuller, recently told the BBC her force has been understaffed and under resourced for years."The facts are the facts," she said. "We have got the highest crime rate in the country. We've had the largest decrease in officers in the country since 2010."As a police force, if you were to look at the multiple indices of deprivation, our police force is number one. So we absolutely need more, we need more resources."An extra £2m targeted funding has since been designated to help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026-2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash.The annual HMIC report comes just months after a different publication by the Police Leadership commission found the system for identifying and developing leaders was too weak, with chief constable roles in England and Wales often attracting a single suitable candidate.The landmark independent review warned police leadership is not consistently of a high enough standard and requires a fundamental overhaul.It also pointed to low morale and motivation within the service, recommending reformed recruitment and promotion processes.Additional reporting by Dan Sales

schema.headline: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says

title: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King
description: King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royalsImage source, ReutersImage caption, The Sussexes' return to the UK will not change their st
body: King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royalsImage source, ReutersImage caption, The Sussexes' return to the UK will not change their status, says Buckingham PalaceByRoyal correspondentThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not be working royals allowed to carry out official engagements now they have returned to the UK, a letter sent on behalf of King Charles spells out.The letter is intended to clarify the status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.It comes as Prince Harry appears to have been pictured for the first time since his return, with a photo on social media showing him at a London TV and podcast studio.Figure caption, What was in the King's letter about Harry and Meghan?The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals."It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case."The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince Harry and Meghan revealed a surprise return to the UK last monthPrince Harry and Meghan faced an acrimonious departure from the UK in 2020, which they chronicled in their Netflix documentary.They established their financial independence in California, including Prince Harry writing a best-selling memoir Spare and Meghan creating an online food range, As Ever.This summer the couple made a surprise return to the UK, where their children will be going to school.It's expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.Disputes about Prince Harry and Meghan's security in the UK remain unresolved and the letter spells out: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."Prince Harry has complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK, but the Palace says that has to be addressed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - which decides security for royals and public figures.Palace sources have suggested it was better to make the Lord Chamberlain's letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.Prince Harry and Meghan's representatives have been contacted for a response.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King

title: Jake and Callum Robinson: Trial over alleged murders of Australian surfer brothers starts in Mexico
description: Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.The bodies of Callum Robin
body: Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California.Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft.The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult"."We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC."Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away."On the opening day, the accused - Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants.Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial.The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada.Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns. The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders.Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader.Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory.Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player.His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding.

schema.headline: Jake and Callum Robinson: Trial over alleged murders of Australian surfer brothers starts in Mexico

title: Prince George to start school at Eton College
description: Prince George set for first day at Eton CollegeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Prince George, pictured last month, will follow in his father'
body: Prince George set for first day at Eton CollegeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Prince George, pictured last month, will follow in his father's footsteps at EtonByRoyal correspondentUpdated 2 hours agoPrince George is taking another step in growing up with his first day at Eton College.He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, who also attended the historic school in Berkshire.The 13-year-old prince will become a boarder at the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around £65,000 a year.As the oldest child of Prince William and Catherine, George is second in line of succession to the throne.Image source, Kensington Palace/Matt PorteousImage caption, A photograph of Prince George was released for his 13th birthdayThere had been speculation about which school Prince George would attend when he finished at independent prep school Lambrook in Berkshire, with a number of private schools being suggested.But a traditional option was chosen, with Prince George following his father, uncle Prince Harry, and great uncle Earl Spencer in attending Eton College.Prince George will now become a boarder, with the school having 25 boarding houses, with each having approximately 55 pupils, looked after by residential staff headed by a house master.The school is also not far from the prince's family home in Windsor.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince William on his first day at Eton in 1995"Some boys take to boarding like a fish to water; others take a minute to settle in," writes the Good Schools Guide about Eton College, which says the school provides each boy with a private single room.Melanie Sanderson, the school guide's managing editor, said Eton has "spectacular facilities and spacious grounds"."Yet despite its ancient buildings, it is a modern school with a progressive outlook."Most 13-year-old boys arriving there in September cannot possibly know what adult life holds for them."Prince George, however, faces a very particular future and his parents, with an unrivalled choice of schools available to them, have decided that an Eton education represents the best preparation for life as a modern working royal," she said.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, William's mother, father and brother, plus house master, on his first day at EtonImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince Harry, with his father and housemaster, arrived at Eton on a rainy day in 1998Among recent politicians to have attended Eton have been Lord David Cameron, Boris Johnson, Kwasi Kwarteng and Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.Old Etonian celebrities include Eddie Redmayne, Dominic West, Damian Lewis and Tom Hiddleston.Prince William, interviewed when he was aged 18, had spoken of enjoying his time at Eton."I've really enjoyed being able to go about Eton as just another student," he said in June 2000.

schema.headline: Prince George to start school at Eton College

title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
description: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetime
body: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer."Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples."It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade."With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here."I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

schema.headline: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant

title: Newcastle were 'preparing for months' for Eddie Howe departure - Ross Wilson
description: Newcastle United sporting director Ross Wilson says the club were preparing for former head coach Eddie Howe's departure for up to nine months.Althoug
body: Newcastle United sporting director Ross Wilson says the club were preparing for former head coach Eddie Howe's departure for up to nine months.Although Howe had originally intended to carry on this season, the drained manager decided to step down in July because he felt it was in the best interests of all parties for him to take a break.It was a summer of huge change, as several key players departed, but Newcastle did not envisage Howe leaving when he did following nearly five years in charge.However, Wilson is adamant the Englishman's exit was not "chaotic" or "painful" because the club had a contingency plan in place, which led to the appointment of Matthias Jaissle."We always knew where we were going to go," Wilson said. "That doesn't mean we were always going to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning."Part of our responsibility as leaders of the club is to be prepared and Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach."That means he was probably going to do something else at some point so we had to be prepared for that."Newcastle spoke to multiple candidates, but Wilson said Jaissle emerged as their first-choice to replace a "legend of the club".The Scot, who was appointed in October, said he had "been planning for a managerial change for eight or nine of those months" in the background.Newcastle's hierarchy always knew they wanted Howe's eventual successor to build on the foundations he put in place with an aggressive, high-pressing playing style.Jaissle also had a history of developing younger players, particularly during his previous spell at Red Bull Salzburg, which aligned with Newcastle's strategy of targeting signings aged 24 and under.Following Wilson's first meeting with Jaissle, who joined from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, Newcastle chief executive David Hopkinson told him he sounded "really excited about this one"."I didn't deliberately go on the phone to do that," Wilson said. "But I remember saying 'you're probably right. I think this is it'."Jaissle remains unbeaten in his first four games in charge of Newcastle in all competitions.However, only three of the club's eight summer signings - Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez - started in the 2-2 draw against Bournemouth.It felt like a reminder of the time it will take some of the new arrivals to bed in during what Jaissle has repeatedly called a "transition phase".Newcastle have forecast a range of financial scenarios, depending on where the club finish this season, but Wilson maintained the German has not been set a specific target for the campaign.Hopkinson, though, reiterated that Newcastle's ultimate ambition is to "consistently and credibly compete" for the top honours in the long run.After entering into a Uefa settlement, following a breach of the European football governing body's financial rules, Hopkinson stressed Newcastle needed to be compliant with the game's regulations to do so.The Magpies have set out to boost revenues by 50% between now and 2030 - mainly through sponsorship deals - but trading players will remain a key part of the club's strategy in order to reinvest."We want to have players here who are on a journey with us," Wilson said. "Equally, if some of those players' journeys go at rapid speed, they might go somewhere else but, of course, that's normal. That's part of football."Although Newcastle had prepared for the departures of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively, the club had never planned to lose talisman Bruno Guimaraes.Newcastle also had to readjust during the window after top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi joined Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.However, aside from Guimaraes going to Arsenal, Wilson claimed "everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan"."That does not mean that every single player [who signed] was the number one name on our list, but that is never the case in any transfer window," he said."Clearly we were disappointed a couple of times but, again, that's normal. "No club goes into the window and reaches the end getting every target they set out to get. If they say they did, it is a lie."

schema.headline: Newcastle were 'preparing for months' for Eddie Howe departure - Ross Wilson

title: Aston Villa: No goals as Unai Emery rebuilds Villa's forward line in a new era
description: Yet, Jackson's time at Bayern Munich - helping them win the Bundesliga last season - gave him a 21.1% conversion rate, scoring eight goals in 1,004 mi
body: Yet, Jackson's time at Bayern Munich - helping them win the Bundesliga last season - gave him a 21.1% conversion rate, scoring eight goals in 1,004 minutes of game time. It is why Emery trusts Jackson, but the unknown is being able to gel a new core of players together, however high their potential. Emery also has to ensure Mbaye - a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain on deadline day - and Garnacho can provide Jackson the ammunition. Between them, Watkins and Rogers scored 46% of Villa's goals in the Premier League last season. Rogers and Lucas Digne provided 12 assists, with Youri Tielemans adding four and Watkins three.All four have left, so 18-year-old Mbaye and Chelsea loanee Garnacho will be expected to be the supply line, with Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham supporting Jackson. Garnacho has, so far, been kept out by George Hemmings - the 19-year-old is highly rated at Villa Park with Emery calling him "clearly a Premier League player".But the academy product only had 25 minutes of top-flight football before this season so expectations must be managed.Argentina winger Garnacho created six big chances, earning four assists, at Chelsea last term but scored just once.Mbaye created four goals in 10 starts for PSG last season, helping them win Ligue 1, and was an unused substitute at Hull on Saturday. Emery will expect more from both once they are in tune with his demands.Manzambi, one of the World Cup's breakout stars in the summer, has yet to play for Villa after his move from Freiburg as he recovers from a knee injury.Emery's messaging is crucial, which is why it will take time for them to develop into the cohesive unit the manager demands. His meetings can last anywhere between 90 minutes and two hours, which naturally tests players' focus levels, but underlines the amount of detail they need to take on board.To integrate 10 new players, including Jackson, Mbaye and Garnacho, takes time. It is time Emery usually likes to use carefully - but it something he does not have in the current circumstances.It is why, when he needed players in January, Douglas Luiz returned on loan from Juventus and Abraham arrived from Besiktas. Luiz knew Emery's methods and Abraham at least knew the club, although neither deal worked - with Luiz returning to Italy and Emery willing to let Abraham go this summer only for the striker to decide to stay.Only two summer signings - Jackson and goalkeeper Zion Suzuki - started the draw at Hull and Taylor Harwood-Bellis was left out of the squad, underlining the situation Emery must deal with."We must be patient, and we should understand that we are rebuilding the team. Now they must get our way and demands, keeping the same mentality that we built, but with different players," said Emery."Now is no time to think two weeks or three weeks forward."We must try to focus on each match. The next match is the Champions League and something we can feel excited and motivated to play because we deserve to be there."Now it is to compete in Brugge on Tuesday. Then, we are going to think about the next match at home against Nottingham Forest."Each match is a lot of information we can have. We are collecting information individually and collectively about the players, about the structure, about the capacity to build the team."Saturday was one point. It was not enough, but I am feeling optimistic about how the players are responding."

title: A&E did not get the basics right - now my son's life is ruined at 32
description: In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches
body: In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness.He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis.Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments.Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history.Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time.Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him. North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it.In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused."An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life."Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families."She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures. "There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A&E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death."A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21.It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550m last year.Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed.And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling.But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts. The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted.The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years. Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged.RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering". "This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing."But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances.NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes.Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses.NHS England said claim numbers were not a good measure of current safety because of the lag between the incident happening and claims being logged, adding there were signs A&E waiting times had started improving.Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short".For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying about his son."I know staff are under pressure," he says, "but this is about doing the basics right. They failed Oli."Additional reporting Nat Wright

title: Champions League 2026-27 predictions: Who will win the title?
description: Julien Laurens: If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already specia
body: Julien Laurens: If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already special - three in a row is impossible unless you've got Cristiano Ronaldo in your team, which they don't.I think they will be close. I think they'll reach at least the semi-final, but I think going for three in a row is tough.I don't believe fully in the Jose Mourinho-Real Madrid project, so I would go for Bayern Munich and Arsenal to reach the final. They are probably the teams, other than PSG, who have deserved to be there the most in the past two seasons. To win it, I'll go for Arsenal. They have the best defence in Europe by far and that's what wins you titles. I would go for PSG to reach the last four, Bayern close runners-up and Arsenal to win it.Guillem Balague:With PSG's irregular start to the season we are seeing how difficult it is to maintain the level. Luis Enrique continues to push the team to be in the vanguard of football which is demanding, with dynamic football and relentless pressure. With the league phase considered a place to experiment and prepare for the second half of the season, there will be a time of transition and strange results before the crunch time in January onwards. As the main axis is there, I expect them to get very close to winning it again.But Barcelona are flying. They would like another centre-back and a number nine. It is what Hansi Flick wanted to get to the next level but he feels they are on the way to the top anyway. Arsenal have found a way to win regularly, and with that off their shoulders, players feel a release that will make them play better. Those three should be in the semis unless they meet before. The fourth, again draw permitting, should be Bayern Munich, Real Madrid or Manchester City.Julien Laurens:I have picked five players to watch in this year's Champions League. The first is Jude Bellingham. This is a very big season for him individually and collectively for Real Madrid under Mourinho in the number 10 role that I think suits him well. After a very good World Cup, I think that momentum will carry. I expect him to score a lot of goals and to be very strong and be decisive.Como's number 10 Nico Paz is at the heart of everything they do with the ball. It's their first time in the Champions League. Cesc Fabregas is the manager, so they're a very entertaining team, nice to watch. Paz is a special player - very much in the making - but he will be a top player very soon.Mr Champions League - Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. In the past two seasons, he's been incredible at PSG, especially last year on that left wing where he can cut inside or go on the outside, he's a threat with the right foot and the left foot, he scored some great goals, he's really good technically. I think he's in the running for the Ballon d'Or. He's one of those players that gets you on the edge of your sofa. He's the guy. Lens are back in the Champions League having pushed PSG all the way last year in Ligue 1 - and Ismaelo Ganiou is arguably their best player. A strong centre-back, 21 years old, good on the ball, very quick and physical. I expect him to leave at the end of the season for a big Premier League club.Since leaving Aston Villa to go to Roma, Donyell Malen has been incredible, scoring almost a goal per game as a lone striker for Gian Piero Gasperini's side. Roma being back in the Champions League is great and they're a very entertaining team to watch again. I think we will see Malen back to his best level.Guillem Balague:Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane is in a campaign to win the Ballon d'Or. He deserves to be in contention and I do not expect him to drop his level as Bayern's style suits him greatly.Teenager Lamine Yamal is hungry for more and has set his sights on the Champions League. Hansi Flick wants a team that defends high and passionately so he can shine.Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has got another level and with PSG going far he will again rescue the team and win big games. He will be a Ballon d'Or winner soon.Shakhtar have a long tradition of converting Brazilian stars into European multimillion transfers and 20-year-old Kaua Elias could be the next one on the list.After a difficult season for Martin Odegaard last year with injuries, he has started this one very well. The Norwegian can dominate games, and his team - more confident now - will need him to do that. He seems ready to take that leadership.According to Opta, last year's runners-up Arsenal are the overall favourites to win the Champions League (20.4%) although Bayern Munich, who lost to PSG in the semi-finals, are only marginally behind (20%).PSG's chances of winning a third European title in a row are 7.3%, fourth overall, while 2023 winners Manchester City are third, having been given a 12.7% chance.All five of the Premier League teams are ranked inside the top 10 for overall win probability and all have been given a more than 50% chance of reaching the last-16.When it comes to the league phase, Liverpool have the easiest draw according to Opta's power rankings while Stuttgart have the easiest run overall and Inter Milan the most favourable of the teams from pot one.Arsenal also have a relatively favourable draw. Despite drawing Real Madrid and Bayern Munich from pot one, Mikel Arteta's side also drew the two lowest-ranked sides in the competition - Sabah and Slovan Bratislava.Manchester City face the toughest fixtures of the English clubs with only five teams receiving a tougher draw overall. They have drawn two European giants from pot one in Barcelona and PSG, while 24th-ranked Napoli are a particularly difficult test from pot three.Last season, Arsenal finished top of the league phase after being given one of the easiest fixture lists according to Opta, while Bayern Munich finished second despite being handed the toughest set of opponents of all 36 sides.

title: Paul Smith: How the designer known for colourful stripes conquered fashion
description: How colourful stripes (and rubber chickens) helped Paul Smith conquer the fashion worldImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Paul Smith is famo
body: How colourful stripes (and rubber chickens) helped Paul Smith conquer the fashion worldImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Paul Smith is famous for his signature stripes and colourful designsByColin PatersonEntertainment correspondentSir Paul Smith, the doyen of British fashion, is flailing around in his office with two large rubber chickens and making them squeak them with gusto."The chickens are the reason I was successful in Japan," he explains."I've been working in Japan since 1982. And when I first went there, there was one person who spoke schoolboy English. So, it was very much about communicating through gesture, drawings, but also humour."Enter the rubber chickens."So, if I was a bit tired at four o'clock in the afternoon, I used to just go into my bag and go..."He demonstrates another squeak."And then everybody collapsed with laughter."It certainly did the trick. Almost 45 years, later there are more than 20 Paul Smith stores in Japan, part of a global empire spanning 50 countries.Sir Paul has invited BBC News to spend an afternoon with him at his London HQ to talk about his new autobiography Threads: My Life in Style. Image caption, Sir Paul Smith's office in central London is packed with books, trinkets, clothing and giftsFirst, he is showing us what he jokingly calls his "minimalist executive suite" where he is surrounded by huge piles of gifts and curiosities, which he is sent every day by fans."For about 45 years, I've been receiving interesting things from a fan in America, and this is one of the latest ones," he says gesturing to a plastic goose covered in stamps with his address written on the side - continuing the plastic poultry theme."They always arrive without a box and there's no message so we're not really sure who they're from."He picks out a few more favourites from what looks like the most jumbled of jumble sales, including a clockwork toy drummer, nativity scenes made out of nuts, and the bike Chris Froome won the Tour De France on.And every morning, after his 0530 swim, he writes a thank you postcard to everyone who has included an address."Good manners is really important in business, especially for longevity," he reflects.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Paul says his "dear lovely wife" Pauline Denyer bought most of the stock on the day he opened his first shop in 1970In many ways, this scene is a perfect example of what has made Sir Paul Smith's career such a stellar one - it represents his enthusiasm for life, combined with his knowledge of what is needed to succeed.These are themes which he investigates in Threads, which tells the tale of how his ambitions to be a professional cyclist were ended by a crash at the age of 17, leading him to explore the world of fashion.He opened his first shop - a tiny, windowless store in Nottingham - in 1970. "The first day I took £38, and my dear lovely wife bought most of it just to please me," he recalls.The decision to write the book was partly inspired by turning 80 and wanting to pass on advice to those wanting to follow him into fashion."I get so many students here, they think, 'I need a fashion show, two shops, a million pounds and everything'. But if you're patient, you can grow slowly and carefully. And that's what I did."More than five decades on from opening his first store, Sir Paul's company has become one of the leading British fashion brands, known for its signature stripes and colourful twists on traditional British tailoring. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Smith pictured on stage at his Paris Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 showImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The fashion brand is known for its signature stripes and colourful twistsThankfully, the book also does not shy away from some serious A-list name-dropping.It turns out that when George Best went missing when he was supposed to be playing for Manchester United, he was often in Sir Paul's spare bedroom.The unlikely pair met in the early 70s when Best had a line of children's clothes and Sir Paul worked for the company which designed them."George famously used to get quite stressed out because he was the first superstar footballer and there was a lot of so-called friends that weren't really friends," he explains."On a Friday, often he would just start to get a bit disturbed. I was sent off in the company's Rolls Royce, with my long hair and velvet trousers to Heathrow VIP area to collect him and then take him to the flat so he could escape for the weekend.""And I don't know anything about football, so we got on really like a house on fire. He said to me, 'Nobody's ever talked to me like this'. We used to have fish and chips."Image source, Paul Smith ArchivesImage caption, Sir Paul was friends with David Bowie and designed a T-shirt to accompany the singer's final albumMusic also features heavily, from the time Sir Paul McCartney made him a cheese sandwich after a soundcheck at the Hammersmith Apollo, through to being friends with David Bowie from the 80s."He was very inquisitive. He used to call me Smithy. He used say, 'Smithy, why have you got that book? What's that there?' He was a very curious man."And things came full circle when Sir Paul was commissioned to design a T-shirt to accompany Bowie's final album Black Star."I had a hint he was ill because he was in Switzerland a lot," he reveals. "So, we lost him for a while."For those who heard Sir Paul Smith on Desert Island Discs in 1992 it may be a surprise that he has written a book at all.When asked to pick his book, he told presenter Sue Lawley: "I have to admit that I'm not a reader at all, because I've got this very, very busy mind and it just leaps around all the time and I just can't hold a book for any length of time."He opted for the 1974 Beano Annual, because it had "16 pages of Roger the Dodger".In Threads, he explains that he is dyslexic and it was undiagnosed throughout his school days."It hasn't impacted me at all. I just can't read very well," he explains. "So when I do talks, which I do quite a lot, I just do it out of my head and hope it sounds all right."Image source, Paul Smith ArchivesImage caption, Sir Paul, pictured in the 1990s, originally wanted to be a professional cyclist Next on the tour we are shown how his famous stripe designs are created by using thread. They first appeared as part of Paul Smith's spring 1992 range, but customer demand quickly led to them coming back."Eventually you think, oh, how many more combinations of a stripe can I do?" he admits, before adding, "But so far so good."Stretching "so far" to 35 years, shows just how much "good" those stipes have brought him.Before leaving, Sir Paul shows us all four storeys of his art wall which wraps around the main staircase (framed pictures, mementos, newspaper cuttings and photos from all aspects of his life) before emerging onto a rooftop garden.Image caption, Sir Paul showed the BBC's Colin Paterson the artworks and newspaper cuttings that cover his office wallsThen finally a walk to the Paul Smith flagship store in Floral Street, where the man with his name on the sign, still tries to work on the floor for a few hours every week."They always claim I'm the best salesman," he laughs. "I have a knowledge about the product, because I designed it, and so I can talk about it."It is great fun watching as customers slowly realise (some with a bit of prompting) that they are talking to THE Paul Smith, with reactions ranging from "I've been shopping here since the 1980s","I love your glasses," to "at least I know you are real and not AI".Finally, it seemed appropriate to round things off by ending where we started, with a gift. I had a specially chosen one for him.As he unwraps it a huge beam of a smile emerges over his face when he realises, he now has a copy of his Desert Island Discs book choice – The 1974 Beano Annual."I haven't got it," he beams. "I mean that's class. Brilliant."Sir Paul Smith says goodbye and heads off back towards his HQ, walking through the sunny streets of Covent Garden with a Beano annual tucked under his arm – a fashion icon who knows all about fun.Threads: My Life in Style by Sir Paul Smith is published on 10 September

schema.headline: Paul Smith: How the designer known for colourful stripes conquered fashion

title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - documentary glosses over the hard stuff
description: "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a
body: "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a power struggle any more."The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus. In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009.Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room"."The band doesn't exist any more," he announces, sounding more irritated than sad.According to Scottish singer Amy McDonald, who was also on the line-up, the altercation was seismic. "Liam smashed Noel's guitar, huuuge fight!" she tweeted from backstage.The film, however, never tells us what was said. Nobody explains the fall-out. We don't find out who instigated the rapprochement, nor do we hear how it affected their family.Instead, we cut to rehearsals for the comeback tour, with a caption informing us the brothers "didn't speak for 15 years", and an implication that all the wounds have been miraculously healed.Tantalisingly, the first song they practice is Columbia - a fan favourite that never made the tour's setlist - but there's a tension in the room. The band, under Noel's instruction, is piecing together the setlist. Liam won't arrive until later in the process, and no-one's sure which Liam they'll get.When he arrives, he seems fantastically grumpy, complaining about the sound-proofing panels that have been placed in front of Joey Waronker's drums."They're already giving me the hump," he huffs. But when he steps up to the mic, the band relax. Guitarist Bonehead - who's strategically placed between Liam and Noel - beams from ear to ear. A couple of hours later, still in the middle of a song, Liam waves goodbye and casually strolls out of the rehearsal space."I'm not sure whether our kid's enjoying himself," Noel says to his bandmates. In a voice-over, Liam reveals, enjoying himself wasn't the goal."If you're not on it, chaos can ensue," he says, adding that he's given up cigarettes and alcohol (the intoxicants, not the song) for the duration of the tour. "These songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect."Liam grabs Noel's hand and thrusts it into the air, they launch into the opening chords of Hello, and the crowd practically explodes with joy. As the gig continues, they dance and cheer and weep. During Slide Away, a man sinks to his knees and sings the lyrics, his hands clasped together as if in prayer. When the gig ends, cameras capture a young fan in an awe-struck stupor, unable to tear himself away from his spot on the stadium floor.This is where the documentary excels - capturing the sheer surge of affection that greeted Oasis's return. We visit shows in Dublin, Manchester, Sao Paolo, Tokyo and New York - and every one has a fan with a personal story to tell.One woman has named her dog Bonehead. Another is a Haenyeo - a South Korean free-diver - who says Oasis's music helped her out of depression. Noel, in particular, is blindsided by the impact."The gravity hit me of what it meant to people and it took me by surprise," he reflects. "I have to say it actually knocked me back."Structurally, though, the film has a problem. In a biopic, the triumphant night in Cardiff would have been the final scene - the moment of resolution after 15 years of pain. Here, it comes about 40 minutes into the action. Every subsequent concert just rinses and repeats the same story. The music is still thrilling. The live mix is impeccable. Liam sounds incredible. But  Southern and Lovelace are left flailing around for a story. In Manchester, they focus on a priest delivering a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. In London, they follow a survivor of the Manchester Arena Bombing, who reflects on the way Don't Look Back In Anger became an anthem of resilience.But the film sidesteps the fact that Liam spent the mourning period criticising his brother for his failure to appear at charity shows supporting the survivors.It's not the only omission. There's no mention of the dynamic pricing row that overshadowed the launch of the tour (although Liam is heard apologising for the lack of "cheap seats" during one of the concerts).And while Noel praises Bonehead's contribution to the band, calling him "the sound of Oasis," we never hear from the guitarist; and the film never addresses his cancer diagnosis, which forced him to miss the final leg of the tour.Sometimes, the filmmakers hint at uncovered stories. Noel mentions missing weeks of rehearsals because of a bad back; and its revealed that the Gallagher brothers' kids met for the first time on the tour - but, for some reason, those threads are left un-pulled. Clearly, a decision was made to concentrate on the music. The cameras don't (or weren't allowed to) follow Liam and Noel off stage. Their joint interview provides a few highlights. Liam's riff on Mick Jagger's creaking limbs is worth the price of admission alone. But you get the feeling that everyone's on their best behaviour for Disney Plus... unless you count the copious swearing.That said, if you attended any of the Oasis '25 shows, this is an incredible souvenir of all the tear-soaked euphoria and musical communion that accompanied their comeback.And, of course, it works as a very effective trailer for the band's much-rumoured return to Knebworth next summer.Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger is in cinemas from Wednesday 9 September.

schema.headline: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - documentary glosses over the hard stuff

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Port in a storm' and 'Megxit means Megxit'
description: Several of Tuesday's papers reflect on the anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth. Metro's headline is "port in a storm", explaining that police we
body: Several of Tuesday's papers reflect on the anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth. Metro's headline is "port in a storm", explaining that police were injured, external and vehicles damaged as hundreds of protesters blocked efforts to bring ashore 120 migrants. The Sun says the "anger of decent, law-abiding folk, external" is rising. "Now they try to stop the lifeboats, external" is the Daily Mirror's take on events, adding that the "mob" targeted "RNLI heroes". The Daily Express urges the government "not to ignore public anger, external over illegal migrants", although its editorial stresses the paper agrees with the police that "violence has no part to play in protest".The Times looks ahead to the government's expected announcement of a trade ban affecting Israeli settlements, external in the occupied West Bank. The paper says retaliation by Israel is likely, as is sharp criticism from the US. The Guardian reports that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also say that the government will take a "more active" approach in supporting the Palestinian cause, external.The i Paper reports the Treasury is to introduce a new ISA, external to help people buy their first home, and that it will not have an age limit. It is believed that the details are likely to be set out by Chancellor John Healey in his upcoming Budget.Many of the papers lead on the King clarifying that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex remain private citizens, after their recent move back to the UK. "No return to the Firm, external" is the Daily Telegraph's headline. The Daily Mail says the King has put "Harry and Meghan in their place, external". "Megxit means Megxit" declares the Sun, external.And the Daily Mirror is one of several papers to have picked up on criticism of US President Donald Trump's proposed new uniform for his Space Force, external. The paper says the look, which features a fitted tunic, peaked cap and knee high boots, have drawn comparisons to a "sinister Star Wars-villain style outfit". The menswear writer Derek Guy is quoted as saying it is the kind of costume designers make to point out "who are the bad guys in a space movie". The Daily Star's headline is "storm bloopers, external".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Port in a storm' and 'Megxit means Megxit'

title: US Open 2026 results: Coco Gauff beats Iva Jovic & Elena Rybakina sweeps aside Naomi Osaka to complete stacked New York quarter-finals draw
description: It was not so long ago that Coco Gauff was the teenage sensation looking to cause an upset at the US Open.Now, at the grand old age of 22, she is the
body: It was not so long ago that Coco Gauff was the teenage sensation looking to cause an upset at the US Open.Now, at the grand old age of 22, she is the Grand Slam champion and leading WTA Tour star who drew on her experience to deal with talented 18-year-old Iva Jovic at Flushing Meadows.Fourth seed Gauff found her finest level of the fortnight to beat fellow American Jovic in a 6-1 6-4 win and secure her place in the quarter-finals.Gauff's comfortable progress ensured the top six seeds have reached the US Open women's last eight for the first time since 1998, further illustrating the strength in depth at the top of the WTA Tour.Earlier on Monday, second seed Elena Rybakina swept aside two-time champion Naomi Osaka to also reach the quarter-finals - and close in on becoming world number one.Gauff and Rybakina are among five Grand Slam winners in a strong quarter-final line-up which also features reigning Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen."The women's field is in such a healthy, strong position," former world number five Daniela Hantuchova said on BBC Radio 5 Live."It's one of those tournaments where anyone can take it from here."Jovic is already ranked well inside the top 20 and predicted for even greater things, meaning the fourth-round match was expected to be a serious test for Gauff.The pair immediately put each other under pressure in a physical start to the match, exchanging breaks of serve as the opening three games consisted of 24 points and stretched over 17 minutes.That gave little indication about how quickly Gauff - who could become world number one if she wins the title and Rybakina loses in the quarter-finals - would seize control.Once the 2023 champion broke again for 3-1 she was able to continue pounding Jovic's defence with her consistency from the baseline.Signs of the emotional energy which 14th seed Jovic exerted in her previous victory over her close friend Alexandra Eala - an epic lasting over three hours - started to show as Gauff won 13 of the final 15 points to wrap up the opening set in 33 minutes.But the way Jovic bounced back in a competitive second set illustrated why she is so highly rated.The teenager, who has Serb parents and has been mentored by Novak Djokovic,  showed her mental resolve to fight off four break points and rediscovered her ability to land explosive winners.Jovic could not save a fifth as she trailed 3-2 and although she instantly broke back, Gauff's supreme athleticism and quality continued to wear her more inexperienced opponent down."Iva is an incredible player and an incredible talent, she plays beyond her years," said Gauff, who continues her quest for a third major title against French Open champion Mirra Andreeva on Wednesday."I'm looking forward to many more battles out here, I'm sure we will be playing a lot more matches in the future."Earlier on Monday, Rybakina overpowered 13th seed Osaka to win 6-1 6-4 on Louis Armstrong Stadium and set up a quarter-final against Zheng.Kazakhstan's Rybakina will become the world's leading player for the first time if she reaches the semi-finals in New York, even if top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka goes on to defend her title.China's Zheng came from 5-0 down in the first set of her fourth-round match to beat former champion Iga Swiatek."Of course I want it, I don't know anyone who won't want this," Rybakina said of the number-one ranking."I tried to approach it the same way and do everything I can, and fight to the end of my next match."If I serve as well as I did today, I think I can do well. Let's hope it goes my way."Rybakina, 27, dropped only four points in a near flawless performance on serve against four-time Grand Slam champion Osaka, who said after the match she was struggling with pain in her leg.She faced the 28-year-old full of confidence, having not dropped a set in her opening three matches at the tournament, and took control of the contest in a dominant first set.Reigning Australian Open champion Rybakina opened up a double break over Osaka, before sealing the set in just 21 minutes.Osaka showed greater resistance early in the second set but, after failing to convert her only break point of the match, Rybakina soon seized control again.She broke to go 4-3 up, before safely seeing out the rest of the match, with Osaka unable to contend with her opponent's deep groundstrokes.Rybakina sealed the match inside 66 minutes with her seventh ace of a match where she hit a total of 29 winners to Osaka's nine.Asked about the gap of almost six years since her last major win, at the 2021 Australian Open, Osaka said: "I thought about it, and if I win another Grand Slam, it's not going to change my life."That's kind of crazy that I can say that, because I remember the first Slam that I won, it was, like, a huge whirlwind."

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Coco Gauff beats Iva Jovic & Elena Rybakina sweeps aside Naomi Osaka to complete stacked New York quarter-finals draw
